## 3. Ground Truths

**Five-whys, reduce-to-primitives mode (technique applied).** Claim decomposed: "This assessment format validly measures the target competency." Immediate constituents: (a) the format's success signal is causally dependent on possessing the competency (construct validity); (b) the work is attributable to a specific individual; (c) scoring is comparable across test-takers under equivalent conditions; (d) the format is administrable within actual resource constraints. Branch (a) reduces one level further: "causally dependent" means the task cannot be completed above baseline by a substitute production process (copying, ghostwriting, AI generation) at a rate distinguishable from a person who possesses the competency — this bottoms out at the standard psychometric definition of construct validity (Cronbach & Meehl's framework) and passes the irreducibility test: it is a definition, not a further-reducible empirical claim. Branch (d) reduces to a staffing-hours arithmetic identity, verified directly in chain C5 below. This drill supplies GT-10.

**Provenance summary.** `?`-marked: GT-4, GT-6 (2 of 10). Read-at-source: GT-2 (HEPI blog post, 88%/53% figures quoted directly), GT-3 (Inside Higher Ed 2023 article, <1%→~4% figures quoted directly), GT-5 (PMC commentary article PMC12723506, EEG/recall figures quoted directly), GT-7 (arXiv:2303.11156 abstract page, AUROC-bound and paraphrase-attack findings quoted directly), GT-8 (The Conversation article, UK regulator and smart-glasses figures quoted directly). GT-1, GT-9, GT-10 are analytic/definitional — treated as physical-law-like and requiring no external citation, per the same treatment the methodology gives physical laws.

- **GT-1** A take-home writing/analysis artifact evaluated only on its final text, with no identity or process verification, is informationally identical regardless of who or what produced it — the observable output cannot itself carry a record of its authorship. — source: analytic/definitional (a property of what "final-product-only" observation can and cannot encode); no external citation applicable.

- **GT-2** In a survey of 1,041 UK full-time undergraduates conducted by Savanta for HEPI/Kortext in December 2024, the proportion of students reporting they used generative AI in their assessments rose from 53% (prior year) to 88% (2025). — source: HEPI, "HEPI/Kortext AI survey shows explosive increase in the use of generative AI tools by students" (26 Feb 2025); read-at-source: figures quoted directly from the HEPI blog page, including the survey's methodology note (Savanta, Dec 2024, ~3% margin of error).

- **GT-3** Turnitin publicly claimed a "less than 1%" false-positive rate for its AI-writing detector at launch (April 2023); its own chief product officer subsequently acknowledged a sentence-level false-positive rate of approximately 4%, attributing the gap to real-world use diverging from laboratory testing. — source: Inside Higher Ed, "Turnitin's AI detector: higher-than-expected false positives" (1 June 2023); read-at-source: figures quoted directly from the article.

- **GT-4?** A study evaluating seven widely used GPT-text detectors on 91 TOEFL essays from non-native English speakers and 88 U.S. eighth-grade essays found the detectors accurately classified the native-English essays but produced an average false-positive rate of 61.3% on the TOEFL essays, falling to 11.6% when the same essays were rewritten in more elaborate, AI-typical language. — cited to: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, published in *Patterns* (2023); reported-by-delegate: this analysis located the figure via convergent secondary reporting (CASRAI, ScienceDirect summary, gradpilot) after the cited primary source could not be read directly — **Phase 3 failure record:** attempted `arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02819` (returned non-extractable encoded PDF streams) and `arxiv.org/abs/2304.02819` (abstract omitted the quantitative figure); the ground truth remains `?`-marked and feeds only MEDIUM-or-lower chains (C2).

- **GT-5** In a 2025 MIT Media Lab EEG study (Kosmyna et al., preprint arXiv:2506.08872) of 54 participants writing essays across four sessions, the LLM-assisted group showed up to ~55% reduced neural connectivity across memory/attention/executive networks compared with a brain-only group, the weakest sense of ownership of their work, and impaired recall: 83% could not quote any passage from an essay they had just written with LLM help, and when former LLM users later wrote unaided, 78% still could not quote their own work and showed weaker neural connectivity than participants who had never used AI assistance. — source: PMC commentary article (PMC12723506) discussing the Kosmyna et al. study; read-at-source: figures quoted directly from the PMC page (this is a secondary commentary on the primary preprint, which this analysis did not open directly — disclosed here rather than overclaiming primary-source access).

- **GT-6?** Multiple universities have begun mandating or recommending oral/viva components specifically in response to generative AI: Middlesex University's 2025–2026 Academic Integrity and Misconduct Policy mandates a viva when poor referencing, contract cheating, or AI misuse is suspected, and Stanford's Academic Integrity Working Group (2024–2025) recommends oral exams and in-class formats. — cited to: institutional policy documents and working-group reports; reported-by-delegate: located via web-search synthesis; neither institution's primary document was opened directly by this analysis.

- **GT-7** Sadasivan, Kumar, Balasubramanian, Wang & Feizi ("Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?", arXiv:2303.11156, 2023) prove a formal upper bound on any AI-text detector's AUROC as a function of the total-variation distance between human- and machine-text distributions (AUROC(D) ≤ 1/2 + TV(M,H) − TV(M,H)²/2), and show empirically that a light recursive-paraphrasing attack significantly reduces detection rates across classifier-based, zero-shot, and watermarking-based detectors alike. — source: arXiv:2303.11156; read-at-source: abstract page fetched directly, bound and paraphrasing-attack findings quoted from it.

- **GT-8** The UK's exam regulator recorded 2,225 cases involving mobile phones or smart devices in tertiary and secondary exams in 2025 — 44.3% of all recorded cheating cases; AI-enabled smart glasses, micro-earpieces, and smartwatches with internet-connected AI functions have been documented circumventing in-person, proctored exams in South Korea, Taiwan, India, and China, and are reported as difficult for human invigilators to detect. — source: The Conversation, "Unis are going back to in-person exams. But some students are finding new ways to cheat" (2026); read-at-source: figures and device descriptions quoted directly from the article.

- **GT-9** Network- and device-isolated proctoring blocks a test-taker's access to a cloud-hosted AI assistant only to the extent physical security holds; it does not, by itself, block a locally-cached offline model or a smuggled device, and GT-8 documents that such physical circumvention is already occurring at scale. — source: analytic/technical (a description of what network isolation can and cannot restrict), corroborated empirically by GT-8.

- **GT-10** Construct validity requires that a task's observed success or failure correlate with the test-taker's possession of the targeted competency more than with the test-taker's access to a substitute production process for the same artifact — the standard psychometric definition of construct validity (Cronbach & Meehl framework), reached here by the five-whys reduce-to-primitives drill above. — source: analytic/definitional (foundational psychometric definition); no external citation applicable.

No assumption that received a Discard verdict in §2 appears in this list as a ground truth.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Invest further in AI-text detection as the primary integrity mechanism

**What was tried:** considered recommending continued or heavier investment in commercial AI-text detectors (e.g., mandating Turnitin AI scores as evidence in misconduct proceedings) as the university's primary response.

**Why abandoned:** an absent-fails derivation — this path requires the assumption "detectors can become reliable enough with more investment"; chain C3 shows that assumption is false, since detector accuracy is bounded by a quantity (total-variation distance between human/AI text) that shrinks as generative models improve, so the ceiling itself degrades over time rather than reflecting an engineering gap; chains C2's disparate-impact evidence (GT-3, GT-4?) independently reinforces the same conclusion.

**What it ruled out:** saves a future reviewer from re-proposing "buy a better detector" or "wait for detection to improve" as a durable fix — per C2/C3 that path is foreclosed mathematically, not by current technological immaturity.

### Dead End: Harden timed/proctored exams as the sole universal answer (device-screening or remote AI-proctoring software)

**What was tried:** considered recommending a full reversion to timed, in-person exams as a blanket, single-format solution, optionally hardened with device-screening or third-party remote-proctoring software.

**Why abandoned:** chain C6's trade-off scored a full return to timed exams at 59 against the recommended architecture's 87, driven by weak scores on ecological validity, equity, and wellbeing; chain C4/GT-8 additionally shows incomplete attribution-resistance even after hardening (GT-8 documents circumvention in jurisdictions that already screen for devices). Remote AI-proctoring software inherits GT-8's physical-circumvention weakness while adding its own harms (bandwidth/webcam-access inequity, algorithmic false-flagging of disabled and neurodivergent test-takers) consistent with, though not separately quantified beyond, the Cr-C equity criterion's low score for this option-family.

**What it ruled out:** saves a future reviewer from treating "go back to blue books" or "buy remote-proctoring software" as a low-effort universal fix; it remains a legitimate component for specific competency types (chain C6's timed/closed-condition internal branch) but fails as a universal default.

### Dead End: Increase misconduct penalties without changing the verification mechanism

**What was tried:** considered recommending a deterrence-only response — raising the severity of penalties for AI-assisted misconduct, enforced through the existing detection-based process, without redesigning assessments.

**Why abandoned:** an absent-fails derivation — this requires the assumption that the enforcement mechanism identifying misconduct is itself reliable; chains C2 and C3 show that assumption is false (documented, disparate misclassification rates, and a mathematically falling reliability ceiling), so harsher penalties enforced through the same mechanism raise the cost of a false accusation without raising the true-positive catch rate — the conclusion ("stronger deterrence solves this") does not follow from the false premise.

**What it ruled out:** saves a future reviewer from treating penalty severity as a substitute for a validity fix; the two are orthogonal, and pursuing the former alone increases harm (wrongful high-stakes penalties) without addressing the construct-validity gap chain C1 identifies.

## 6. Conclusion

The chains above converge on a single architecture, with the AI-availability shock's mechanism, competency-dependence, and durability limits made explicit rather than assumed.

**Recommended approach:** Adopt a stakes- and competency-proportional, verification-embedded hybrid assessment architecture: keep distributed, take-home work as the default production mode, but attach a brief, live, unpredictable oral defense whose depth scales with the artifact's stakes (spot-check for low-stakes work, full defense for capstone/high-stakes work), reserve purely timed/closed-book conditions for competencies genuinely well-measured under time pressure (foundational recall, bounded problem-solving), and reserve AI-inclusive redesign — grading judgment and verification of AI output — for courses whose actual target competency is AI-augmented practice itself (chain C6).

**Key insight:** Timed-proctored and take-home are not opposite ends of an AI-resistance spectrum — both are arms races between an enforcement mechanism and a concealment/evasion technology, one fought in the text domain and one fought in the physical/device domain; neither is a stable anchor, so the real design problem is which verification mechanism degrades slowest and is cheapest to keep refreshed (chains C2, C3, C4, C7).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The recommended architecture accepts a real, unresolved equity cost from live verbal performance under pressure (chain C6). It accepts a real feasibility/resourcing cost at large-enrollment scale that requires new staffing or an explicit sampling rate rather than a free lunch (chain C5). And it accepts that it is a durable improvement rather than a permanent fix, requiring an ongoing institutional maintenance cadence — question-bank refresh, adaptive questioning, disaggregated-outcome monitoring — as a standing operational requirement, not an afterthought (chain C7).
